transcript: The foot of Snowdon, where rocks rear themselves in fantastic piles, even to the clouds.
The expanding hills, cast in a broader and deeper shade.
Their majestic, dark brown foregrounds, their grey or purple summits.
Here the dense wood, and there the purple heath.
There, where the race of man appears to be extinct, where not a tree, nor shrub, nor cottage will remind you of humanity.
Where no sound is heard, but the rushing of waters, the union of stream, lake and fall.
On the distant hill, the beautifully variegated foliage of the trees.
Fragrant dew, yet glittering on herb and flower.
The early morning song of birds.
Winds whistling through the mountain hollows.
Under the thousand changing hues, the now soft, now brilliant touches.
Those deeper, mingling lights, and shadows of the falling year.
The lover of science, the botanist, the angler, the artist, the antiquary, or the geologist.
Find more pleasing occupation for their several dispositions.
Scarcely in all nature can a scene,
or truly grand, be witnessed in this imprisoned paradise.
Of which man has never yet presumed to touch.
